questions.q: What is active geo-replication, in plain terms?
options: Azure SQL Database's built-in DR feature: a continuously-updated, readable secondary database in a different Azure region
A backup type that runs nightly against the same region
A feature that only exists for SQL Server on Azure VMs, not Azure SQL Database
A synchronous replication mechanism guaranteeing zero data loss across regions
questions.explain: Active geo-replication is Azure SQL Database's own cross-region DR mechanism, keeping a readable secondary continuously updated in another region.

questions.q: Why is active geo-replication always asynchronous, with no synchronous option?
options: Because waiting for cross-region confirmation on every write would be impractical given the distance between regions
Because Microsoft disabled synchronous replication for licensing reasons only
Because asynchronous replication is actually faster to configure in the portal
Because Azure SQL Database does not support any form of replication
questions.explain: The physical distance between regions makes synchronous cross-region confirmation on every write impractical, so geo-replication is asynchronous by design.

questions.q: Given that geo-replication is always asynchronous, what is the realistic best-case RPO it can deliver?
options: Seconds to low minutes — not zero
Exactly zero data loss, guaranteed
24 hours, matching a nightly backup
There is no way to estimate an RPO for geo-replication
questions.explain: Because it's asynchronous, some very recent transactions can be lost if the primary fails before the secondary catches up, putting the realistic RPO at seconds to low minutes.

questions.q: Besides disaster recovery, what is one genuine real-world use for a geo-replicated secondary, per this lesson?
options: Offloading reporting/analytics workloads to the secondary, or serving low-latency reads to users in a different geography
Running write transactions directly against the secondary during normal operation
Secondaries have no use at all outside of an actual disaster
Storing full and differential backups instead of transaction logs
questions.explain: Because up to 4 geo-secondaries are readable at all times, they can serve reporting workloads or nearby users without touching the primary's write path.

questions.q: How does promoting a geo-replicated secondary to primary happen today, without a failover group layered on top?
options: It's a manual, explicit failover that a DBA initiates
It happens automatically the instant the primary becomes unreachable
It is not possible to promote a secondary under any circumstances
Only Microsoft support can perform this action
questions.explain: Without a failover group, promoting a secondary to primary is a deliberate, manual action — automatic promotion and endpoint management are what failover groups add.
